reasons: You and your partner both log in and share the same data, so it needs a real server-side database from the start — Next.js gives you the app and the API in one project, with Prisma/Postgres as the shared store
Your core flow is CSV in → categorised → 'where my money goes', which is import-parse-persist-render — exactly the full-stack path Next.js handles end to end
Vitest covers the parse/categorise logic fast, and Playwright can watch the real 'import one CSV row and see it on screen' slice run in a browser — a human can literally watch the test go green
It's one TypeScript codebase, so budgets, charts and bank sync later slot in without bolting a backend on afterwards
rec.slice: importing one CSV row and showing it on screen
deferred: Real categorisation rules (beyond one hardcoded rule for the slice)
Multi-user auth and account management polish

rec.idea: a website that does personal finance stuff

question.text: Last thing before I recommend a stack. For the ONE thin vertical slice that proves the skeleton and the tests are genuinely wired together, my recommendation is: importing a single CSV row and showing it categorised on screen — it touches upload → parse → persist → render in one line, and a test can watch that whole path. I'd keep categorisation dead-simple for the slice (one hardcoded rule, e.g. contains "COFFEE" → "Dining"), with real category logic deferred. Does that slice work as the proof, or would you rather the foundation prove a different path (e.g. just persisting a manually-typed transaction)?
choices: Import one CSV row and show it categorised
Manually add one transaction and show it
question.recommended: Import one CSV row and show it categorised
